tier_reason: README Benchmarks table shows the exact wall times (CPath 0.082-0.083s vs find 0.147s, os.walk 0.237s, Cute Files 0.284s, TinyDir 0.294s) with CPU (MacBookAir7,2, Intel Core i5 1.6GHz) and -O3 stated. Benchmark sources are in tests/ (tests.c, cbench.h, benchmark_recursive.py), but no compiler is named, so it is first-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Wall time 0.082-0.083s for CPath (recursion/emplace, C and C++) vs 0.147s for `find`, 0.237s for Python os.walk, 0.284s for Cute Files, 0.294s for TinyDir, 0.626s for `tree`. That is roughly 1.8x faster than `find` and ~3.4-3.6x faster than Cute Files/TinyDir (derived from page data). The project says CPath 'is often around 3x faster than other libraries and even faster than `find`'.
corrections.caveats: The published benchmark compares against `find`, TinyDir, Cute Files, Python os.walk and `tree`, not against std::filesystem, and the README says it is NOT a std::filesystem replacement. So this is evidence against a related but different incumbent (baseline_in_list=false). The benchmark is first-party, on one machine, and names no compiler. The benchmark sources are in tests/ (tests.c, cbench.h, benchmark_recursive.py). The last commit on the default branch (master) is 2019-09-28. The 2023-09-24 date is an unmerged side-branch commit (BraedonWooding-remove-unnecessary-check).

notes: The numbers and hardware check out. The record's last_commit came from the repo's pushed_at, which reflects an unmerged side branch; master was last touched in 2019-09, so it is now abandoned. The ratios were not marked as derived, so claimed_speedup was reworded to add that marker.

tier_reason: The README 'Test results' block shows CFileHandler 56700 ns vs std::ifstream 241000 ns from the public Google Test code in FastReaderTest/test.cpp. It states no CPU, no build configuration (Debug /Od vs Release) and no flags, so it is first-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: CFileHandler: 56,700 ns vs std::ifstream: 241,000 ns, about 4.25x faster (derived from page data). Each figure is the mean of 10 timed samples, and each sample is 3 full line-by-line passes over the 9 KB TestFile.txt. The repo description, not the README, says 'almost 5 times faster than standard C++ std::ifstream'.
corrections.workload: Iterating the lines of a memory-mapped file (CreateFileMapping/MapViewOfFile + memchr, WinAPI) vs std::getline on a std::ifstream. The input is the repo's 9,194-byte TestFile.txt. The Google Test 'Timing' tests in FastReaderTest/test.cpp average 10 samples of 3 passes each, and opening/mapping the file is outside the timed region. The README shows the output of one execution of those tests.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: MSVC, Visual Studio 2019 toolset v142 (per FastReaderTest.vcxproj). The Debug configs use /Od; the Release configs define NDEBUG with no explicit optimization override. Which configuration produced the README numbers is not stated.
corrections.caveats: The numbers come from one execution of a small Google Test timing test (mean of 10 samples x 3 passes over a ~9 KB file), with no stated CPU and no stated build configuration. A Debug build of the MSVC STL would inflate the std::ifstream time. The library is Windows-only (WinAPI memory mapping), so the baseline is the MSVC STL's std::ifstream. Small single-maintainer project with no commits since November 2019.

notes: The numbers match the README. The 'almost 5 times' wording is from the GitHub repo description, not the README. The workload is tiny (9 KB file) and the build configuration is unknown, so treat the 4.25x as weak evidence. The metadata (GPL-3.0, 5 stars, last commit 2019-11-13) is correct.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. The benchmark code is public (benchmarks/periodic_calls.cpp, call_burst.cpp, write_files.cpp, benchmark_mandelbrot.cpp), built via benchmarks/Tupfile.lua + Tuprules.lua, which uses g++ -O3 -std=c++11 for non-DEBUG Linux builds. doc/performance.md states gcc 7.3.0 and an AMD Ryzen 7 2700X, and runs directly against std::fstream and stdio. The 'first-party caps at C' reasoning in the record misreads the rules, which say who ran the benchmark does not matter.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Relative average call latency (reckless = 1.00). Periodic calls: fstream 41.32, stdio 43.77, spdlog 40.85, boost_log 67.42, g3log 78.19. Call burst: spdlog 1.93, fstream 2.36, stdio 2.55. Disk I/O: stdio 17.01, spdlog 23.82, fstream 5719.93. Mandelbrot overhead: single thread fstream 10.73, stdio 12.21, spdlog 9.21; 8 threads fstream 4.62, stdio 3.70. The page concludes: 'For low loads, the speed advantage over a simple fprintf can be a factor of 40.'
corrections.workload: Caller-side log-call latency in four scenarios. (1) Single-threaded periodic calls that never fill the buffer. (2) A call burst that fills the buffer. (3) Disk I/O: 2048 log entries interleaved with writing 64 GiB of data. (4) A Mandelbrot computation that logs ~1M lines with 1-8 worker threads (total runtime over 100 runs, overhead vs no-op). Baselines are std::fstream (std::flush after each line) and fprintf (fflush after each call), plus spdlog, g3log and Boost.Log.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 7.3.0 (stated on the benchmark page). The benchmarks are built with tup (benchmarks/Tupfile.lua + Tuprules.lua), which on Linux compiles with g++ -O3 -ggdb3 -std=c++11 -Wall -Werror unless DEBUG=yes (then -O0). The page itself does not restate the flags.
corrections.caveats: The benchmark is first-party. reckless is asynchronous (formatting and writing happen on a background thread), while the fstream/stdio baselines flush after every line. So the win is caller-side latency under an async-vs-synchronous-flush design, not raw I/O throughput. The figures use 2019-era versions of the competitors (spdlog 1.3.1, g3log 1.3.2, Boost 1.65). GitHub's license detector reports NOASSERTION, but LICENSE.txt is standard MIT text. The last commit on master is 2021-04-10 (a 'next' branch has 2022-07-17 commits); the repo's pushed_at of 2023-10-22 matches no branch head.

notes: The record wrongly said fstream was not in the disk-I/O scenario; it is, at 5719.93x relative latency. The A tier assumes the published runs used the default non-DEBUG tup build (-O3); the page does not say so explicitly. The master branch was last committed in 2021-04, so it is abandoned, not stale.

tier_reason: A peer-reviewed paper (IEEE TPDS vol. 31 no. 6, June 2020; arXiv 2001.09258) gives Table 2 reciprocal throughputs for SLEEF vs scalar FDLIBM 5.3, with gcc-7.3.0 -O3 -mavx2 -mfma on an i7-6700 with Turbo off. The Table 2 harness is not published: SLEEF 3.4.0's src/libm-benchmarks has only SLEEF/SVML benches, not FDLIBM, and master no longer has that directory. So it is not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Table 2, reciprocal throughput in ns per call, 1-ulp variants. SLEEF is the 256-bit AVX2 vectorized function (each call evaluates 4 doubles); FDLIBM 5.3 is scalar (1 value per call). sin [0,1e+100]: FDLIBM 162.3 vs SLEEF 48.79 (~3.3x per call). cos [0,1e+100]: 162.1 vs 50.38 (~3.2x). tan [0,1e+100]: 177.0 vs 48.82 (~3.6x). log [0,1e+300]: 31.66 vs 15.46 (~2.0x). exp [-700,700]: 12.19 vs 7.663 (~1.6x). pow: 69.40 vs 55.53 (~1.25x). On the fast-path domain [0.4,0.5], scalar FDLIBM is FASTER per call (sin 4.927 vs 11.43, cos 11.42 vs 13.75, tan 7.819 vs 17.30), as it is for acos (12.07 vs 16.09) and atan (10.16 vs 22.12). Per element (dividing by 4 lanes), SLEEF is faster in every 1-ulp row. (derived from page data)
corrections.workload: Reciprocal throughput (ns per call) of 256-bit vectorized double-precision SLEEF 3.4 (plus Vector-libm and Intel SVML) vs scalar FDLIBM 5.3. A single-threaded tight loop makes 10^10 calls over pre-generated, uniformly random arguments in each listed domain. The calling loop was compiled without optimization so calls are not elided (the libraries use their -O3 flags), and it is timed with clock_gettime.
corrections.caveats: Table 2 compares SLEEF's 4-wide AVX2 vector functions against scalar FDLIBM. It is not a like-for-like scalar replacement of std::sin/std::exp: the gains need vectorized call sites, and SLEEF's scalar entry points are not in the table. Per call, FDLIBM beats vector SLEEF on narrow-domain sin/cos/tan and on acos/atan. FDLIBM is a reference libm, not glibc's libm or the libm behind libstdc++/libc++/MSVC <cmath>. The benchmark loop was built unoptimized for every library alike. The sleef.org benchmark page compares only against SVML. The Table 2 harness for FDLIBM is not in the repo.

notes: The record misread Table 2. Its 'narrow domain parity, sin 11.43 vs 11.41' pairs two SLEEF cells (the [0.4,0.5] and [0,6.28] rows); the actual FDLIBM value for narrow-domain sin is 4.927, so FDLIBM wins per call there. The record also hid that the comparison is SIMD-vs-scalar. The tier stays B; the verdict is downgrade because the claim needed substantive correction. The metadata (BSL-1.0, 853 stars, last commit 2025-12-25, active) is correct.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. The public benchmark code bench/fast_math_bench.cpp (CMake target fast_math_bench, -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops for both sides) produces the README tables. The Raspberry Pi 4 (Cortex-A72) column states compiler GCC 12.2, the flags and the CPU, and raw output is in sample_result/. The x86 column alone would not qualify: it ran on WSL2 with no CPU model.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Scalar float calls vs std:: (glibc) at identical flags, x86_64 / Raspberry Pi 4. sinh 2.96x/3.94x, tanh 2.94x/3.91x, atanh 2.42x/2.49x, atan2 2.18x/1.63x, integer pow base^2 2.02x/4.54x, acos 1.76x/1.57x, log10 1.45x/2.20x, tan 1.44x/1.40x. 21 of 28 scalar measurements match or beat std on each platform. Slower cases: sincos [-2pi,2pi] 0.88x/0.63x, sin [-2pi,2pi] 1.03x/0.73x, cos [-2pi,2pi] 1.04x/0.82x, sincos [-pi,pi] 0.71x on the Pi, fractional pow 0.84x/0.90x. exp/log/log2/sqrt are 0.94x-1.01x because they forward to std. Batch API vs std loops: atan2 6.16x/3.48x, sincos vs std::sin+std::cos 3.84x/1.97x, sin 2.15-2.28x on x86 but only 0.98-1.06x (parity) on the Pi.
corrections.baseline: <cmath> single-precision (float) overloads (std::sinh, std::tanh, std::atanh, std::atan2, std::pow, std::acos, std::log10, std::tan, std::exp, std::log, etc.), backed by glibc libm (sinhf, tanhf, ...)
corrections.workload: 1,000,000 scalar single-precision (float) calls per function across 28 function/domain combinations (trig, hyperbolic, exp/log family, pow, rounding). Each result is the best of 25 runs with the two implementations interleaved run by run. Benchmarked on x86_64 (GCC 11.4, WSL2) and Raspberry Pi 4 (GCC 12.2); the Pi column takes the minimum over two recorded runs. A batch/array API (1M elements per call) for sin/cos/sincos/atan2 is measured separately.
corrections.hardware: x86_64: WSL2 (Linux 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2), GCC 11.4, CPU model not stated. Raspberry Pi 4 (Cortex-A72): Linux 6.12 aarch64, GCC 12.2.
corrections.caveats: The API is float-only, so the baseline is the float std:: overloads (glibc *f functions), not double precision. The x86 column ran under WSL2 with no stated CPU model. The README warns that run-to-run variance is 5-10% and that some Pi std-library rows moved up to ~70% between runs. The batch sin API is only at parity with std::sin on the Pi. Very small personal project (2 stars). The README is unusually open about parity and slower cases.

notes: The numbers match the README and sample_result/x86_bench_result.txt. The record overstated the batch API as '2-6x' on both platforms, but batch sin on the Pi is 0.98-1.06x. Tier raised to A on the strength of the Raspberry Pi 4 results; the metadata (MIT, 2 stars, last commit 2026-07-28, active) is correct.
